reading.body:
Csquare SFO1 publishes 129.4 MW of combined utility power across 273,000 square feet of technical space in Santa Clara. The specification does not break that figure into IT load versus overhead, so a direct translation requires an assumption: if IT load runs at roughly 60 percent of utility draw, a common rule of thumb for facilities without a published PUE, that implies around 77 MW of IT capacity. At 40 kW per rack, a density typical of current GPU clusters, 77 MW supports roughly 1,900 racks. At 10 kW per rack, a density more typical of general enterprise compute, the same power supports around 7,700 racks. Csquare has not published a rack count or a PUE figure, so neither translation is the operator's claim.

The six certifications collectively qualify SFO1 to host regulated and sensitive workloads. SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2 cover financial and operational controls audited over time rather than at a point in time. PCI DSS qualifies the facility for payment card data. ISO 27001 is an internationally recognized information security management standard. NIST 800-53 aligns the facility with US federal security control frameworks. LEED documents a recognized approach to energy and environmental design. Which tenants or workloads are actually present is not published.

Within California, this site ranks eighth by published megawatts among the facilities this site has read, out of 103 mapped facilities in the state, only seven of which have published a megawatt figure at all. The seven facilities with published figures sum to 185 MW, meaning SFO1's 129.4 MW represents roughly 70 percent of that published total on its own. That concentration reflects the limits of what is published rather than a complete picture of California's data center capacity, and the 96 mapped facilities with no published figure could collectively dwarf the seven that do.
